instruction: I'm learning about forces in school and I'm having a bit of trouble understanding Newton's laws of motion. Can you explain the first law to me?
reply: The first law says a thing keeps still, or keeps going in a straight line at the same speed, unless a force acts on it - which is why a passenger is thrown forward when a bus brakes, and why a seatbelt is the force that stops them. The second law is the useful one: force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma, so the same push moves a light thing quickly and a heavy one slowly, and a 1,000 kg car pushed with 2,000 N accelerates at 2 m/s each second. The third law says every force has an equal force back the other way: you push the ground and it pushes you forward, a rocket throws gas down and the gas throws the rocket up.

instruction: I'm having trouble sleeping at night. Do you have any bedtime routine suggestions?
reply: Fix the wake-up time first: the same hour every day, including after a bad night, and the rest tends to follow within a fortnight. Then the three that do most of the work - daylight and a walk in the first hour, no caffeine after lunch, and a screen-free half hour before bed - and only get into bed when you are sleepy rather than tired. Waking in the small hours is usually the mind, not a sleep problem: keep the room dark, don't check the clock, and after about twenty minutes get up and sit somewhere dim until you are sleepy, so the bed stops being the place you lie and argue with yourself. Still broken after six weeks of that is worth a word with a GP.

Then vary the sentence length - short where it is tense, longer where it is calm - and read it aloud, because the sentence you stumble on is the one to fix. That is three passes, and they fix most flat writing.

instruction: I'm having trouble sleeping at night. What is insomnia?
reply: The things that work: same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after early afternoon, not much alcohol in the evening (it wakes you in the second half of the night), a cool dark room, and getting out of bed if you're awake for more than 20 minutes. Screens off half an hour before bed and a short walk most days help more than any app. If you're worn out all day too, or it has gone on for weeks, ask a GP: they can check your bloods, and broken sleep plus no energy is worth ruling out.

instruction: I'm learning about rocks in school, and I was wondering what the main types of rocks are.
reply: The rock cycle is rocks being made, broken down and made again. Magma cools to igneous rock such as granite or basalt; wind and water wear any rock into grains that settle, get squashed and cement into sedimentary rock such as limestone and sandstone; heat and pressure bake or squeeze rock into metamorphic rock such as marble, from limestone, or slate, from shale. Bury it deeper and it melts back to magma: the three types are one loop, not three separate things.

instruction: I'm having trouble sleeping at night. Do you have any suggestions on how to improve my bedroom environment for better sleep?
reply: Fix the wake-up time first: the same hour every day, including after a bad night, and the rest tends to follow within a fortnight. Still broken after six weeks of that is worth a word with a GP.

instruction: I'm worried about the security of my phone apps. What can I do to keep them safe?

instruction: What is a fraction?
reply: A fraction is a part of a whole written as one number over another: the bottom says how many equal pieces the whole is cut into and the top says how many of those you have, so 3/4 is three pieces out of four. The one thing that trips people up is that the same amount has lots of names - 2/4 is 1/2, and 0.5 is 1/2 too - which is why you can simplify and compare them by putting them over the same bottom number.

instruction: I'm interested in learning about different types of rocks. What's the main difference between igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks?
reply: The rock cycle is rocks being made, broken down and made again. Magma cools to igneous rock such as granite or basalt; wind and water wear any rock into grains that settle, get squashed and cement into sedimentary rock such as limestone and sandstone; heat and pressure bake or squeeze rock into metamorphic rock such as marble, from limestone, or slate, from shale. Bury it deeper and it melts back to magma: the three types are one loop, not three separate things.

instruction: I'm interested in gardening. What are some easy plants to care for?
reply: Water when the top couple of centimetres of compost is dry, not on a fixed day, and let it drain away rather than sitting in water. Most houseplants die of too much water rather than too little: a pot with no drainage hole, or a saucer left full, rots the roots and the leaves go yellow and drop. If the compost smells sour, repot in fresh compost and water less; if it is bone dry and light, soak the pot in a bowl for ten minutes. Beyond that it is light - most want a bright spot out of direct sun - and a feed every few weeks in spring and summer only.

instruction: I'm learning about motion in physics class and I was wondering, what is velocity?
reply: Velocity is how fast you are going and which way: 50 mph north is a velocity, and 50 mph on its own is a speed. So a car going round a roundabout at a steady 30 mph has a constant speed and a changing velocity, because the direction keeps changing. Speed is distance over time, and average speed is the whole trip's distance over the whole time, which is why a two-hour journey with a stop does not average the speed you had on the motorway.

instruction: I have a gluten intolerance and I'm looking for some breakfast ideas.
reply: Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the lining of the gut - not an allergy, and it does not go away; the treatment is a strict gluten-free diet for life, and the gut heals over a few months of it. Strict, and that means being careful about the crumbs in a shared kitchen: a separate toaster, no knife going back in the butter or the jam, no chips from a fryer that has fried battered fish, oats only when the packet says gluten free, and a check on stock cubes, gravy, soy sauce and sausages. There is no cheat day: a little gluten keeps the gut inflamed even when you feel nothing, and the damage builds up quietly. Eating out works if you say coeliac when you book and ask what else goes in the fryer - restaurants that cook from scratch are easier than ones that assemble, and a takeaway with no answer is not worth it. Ask the GP for a dietitian once, and the pharmacist whether a tablet is safe. If it is a suspicion rather than a diagnosis, have the blood test before you cut gluten from your diet, because it only works while gluten is still in it.

instruction: I'm planning to host a party for my friends and I want to cook for them, but I'm not sure where to start.
reply: Count the people first, because it decides the room and the food: 8 to 12 is easy to cook for at home, 30 to 40 is about as many as a house takes, and a pub's back room or a restaurant takes 20 to 60 for a similar price to a hall. Pick the day and send one message with the date, time, place and whether it is a meal or drinks, because "let me know if you can make it" gets half-answers. Keep the food to things made the day before - a pie or a chilli kept warm, a baked ham, bread, two salads and a bought cake - and give two people one job each, drinks and cards and the speech, so you are not doing all of it. Send the invitations three to four weeks ahead, six for a big do or a date near Christmas, and ask for replies by a date a week before. Budget £10 to £15 a head for a buffet at home and £25 to £40 in a restaurant's back room, drink on top.

reply: A simile compares one thing to another with like or as (her laugh was like a kettle, as busy as a bee). A metaphor skips those two words and says the thing is the other one (her laugh was a kettle). Both paint a picture; the simile keeps the comparison out in the open.

instruction: I'm looking for some ideas for break activities at work. Do you have any suggestions?
reply: Count the people first, because it decides the room and the food: 8 to 12 is easy to cook for at home, 30 to 40 is about as many as a house takes, and a pub's back room or a restaurant takes 20 to 60 for a similar price to a hall. Pick the day and send one message with the date, time, place and whether it is a meal or drinks, because "let me know if you can make it" gets half-answers. Keep the food to things made the day before - a pie or a chilli kept warm, a baked ham, bread, two salads and a bought cake - and give two people one job each, drinks and cards and the speech, so you are not doing all of it. Send the invitations three to four weeks ahead, six for a big do or a date near Christmas, and ask for replies by a date a week before. Budget £10 to £15 a head for a buffet at home and £25 to £40 in a restaurant's back room, drink on top.
